newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Business seen as usual despite KL-Singapore row.
newsitem.headline: Business seen as usual despite KL-Singapore row.

text.p: The latest spat between Malaysia and Singapore may be more rhetoric than substance with the economic stakes too high for both sides to ignore, analysts and economists said on Thursday.
They expect business dealings between the two neighbours to continue as usual, with both shying away from actually hurting each other's bottom-line.
"(The row) may affect sentiment, but I don't think it will have a deep dollar impact," said Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers in Kuala Lumpur.

Added a Kuala Lumpur-based foreign fund manager: "Most of this is political rhetoric... On the business-to-business front it is all a bit of a joke. Meetings between Singapore and Malaysian businessmen have resulted in gentle leg-pulling, but nothing more."

The national news agency Bernama and Malaysian daily newspapers quoted unidentified ministers as saying on Wednesday that fresh initiatives with Singapore would be suspended, including the granting of contracts to Singaporean firms.
The reason was Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew's comments about Malaysia's Johor state.
But on Thursday, Malaysia's foreign minister denied there had been a decision to freeze ties with Singapore.
Analysts said the two countries would ignore at their own peril the intertwined business interests.

Singapore is the biggest investor in Malaysia, ploughing $1.3 billion into that country last year. It is also Kuala Lumpur's biggest trading partner, with two-way trade worth $3.74 billion in January this year.
Singapore gets most of its water from Malaysia and sells some of the processed water back to its larger neighbour.
Analysts estimate that Malaysia ships up to half of its exports through Singapore, although Malaysia is building up its ports in competition.

Singapore's financial services sector markets Malaysia to the world. Singaporeans are among the most avid investors in Malaysian stocks through Singapore's over-the-counter market of Malaysian shares.
Ordinary Malaysians help Singapore's economy, with thousands working in the city-state's electronics factories and shipyards.

A research company, Independent Economic Analysis Holdings (I.D.E.A.), said Singapore's dependence on Malaysia has increased in the past decade, with 18 percent of its exports going to Malaysia against 13 percent in 1980. On the other hand, 20 percent of Malaysian exports end up in Singapore.
"This economic inter-dependence suggests that Malaysia would think twice about materially hurting Singapore," I.D.E.A. said.

"It is a rather different situation from the bust-ups between Malaysia and the U.K, and Malaysia and Australia, when the Mahathir regime felt it had little to lose by imposing economic sanctions," the firm said in a commentary.
